label: Spring under tension
summary: Garage door torsion springs, door cables, vehicle coil springs and other large springs store enough energy to break bones, cut and kill when released. The danger is greatest when you loosen something you didn't realise was holding a spring.
signs: Garage doors: a thick coil spring on a bar above the door, or long springs along the side tracks
Steel cables running from the bottom corners of a door to drums or pulleys at the top
Vehicle suspension struts and coil springs
Recoil starter springs in small engines
Heavy springs in machines, trampolines, door closers and lifting arms
do: Leave garage door springs, cables, drums and bottom brackets alone
Take the parts that aren't under tension, such as the opener head unit and wiring
Take car struts out as a whole unit, with the spring still on it
Keep your face and body out of line with any spring you work near
dont: Don't loosen set screws on a torsion spring or its winding cone
Don't unbolt the bottom brackets or cables of a garage door
Don't use screwdrivers or bars that weren't made for winding springs
Don't take a strut apart without a proper spring compressor and training
Don't stand in front of a spring while releasing anything
Don't unbolt a suspension arm, ball joint or axle with a coil spring sitting on it, and don't cut or heat a spring that is still compressed
Don't pull the opener's emergency release or unbolt the opener while the door is open: with a weak or broken spring the door can crash down
ppe: Safety glasses, with a face shield over them
firstAid: A blow to the head followed by confusion, vomiting, drowsiness or unequal pupils needs urgent medical care
Splint suspected broken bones and get medical help
